passage:
After Jonas told her by the bike racks that he just wanted to be friends, Astrid cycled home through the sleet in Gothenburg without her gloves. She didn't text him. She didn't post anything. She sat at her desk with her grandmother's old notebook and wrote until her hand cramped. A poem about a lighthouse that nobody visited. Another about the bike racks, with every bike leaving but one.
On Saturday, her friend Ingrid read them at the kitchen table over cinnamon buns. "These are really good," Ingrid said quietly. "Sad, but good."
Astrid looked at the page. It still hurt. But the hurt had edges now, a shape she could hold up and show someone. That evening she signed up for the school poetry night.

qa.q: What did Astrid's first poem describe?
qa.a: A lighthouse that nobody visited.

qa.q: Why did Astrid write instead of texting Jonas or posting something?
qa.a: She was hurt, and writing let her give the pain a shape without lashing out at him or exposing it online.

qa.q: Which choice turned Astrid's pain into something she could share?
qa.a: Letting Ingrid read the poems, and then signing up for the poetry night, so others could see the feeling she had shaped.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Ingrid to read the poems?
qa.a: Ingrid got to understand how much Astrid was hurting without having to ask, and could answer with honest, gentle praise.

grounding: A teenager in Sweden turned down by a boy writes poems instead of lashing out, and sharing them gives her hurt a shape.

passage:
The school magazine box sat outside the library, and Maria walked past it three times on Monday. Last week Neil had laughed when her friend passed him her note, and said "No thanks" loud enough for half of Class 10 to hear. Maria hadn't said a word to him since. She hadn't cried at school either. Instead, every free period, she sat in the library corner filling a notebook: a song about a bus stop, a poem about a door that only opened one way.
On Monday she tore out the door poem and dropped it into the box. Two weeks later, Simran Ma'am called her to the staff room. "This one's going on page four," she said. "It's honest." Maria went pink, and then, for the first time in days, she smiled.

qa.q: Where did Maria drop the door poem?
qa.a: Into the school magazine box outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Maria fill a notebook instead of saying anything to Neil?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed after the public 'No thanks', and writing gave the pain a shape without lashing out.

qa.q: Which choice was the turning point for Maria, and what came of it?
qa.a: Tearing out the door poem and putting it in the magazine box; it let others see her feeling and brought Simran Ma'am's praise.

qa.q: How might Simran Ma'am see the door poem?
qa.a: She sees honest writing worth publishing, and may sense real feeling behind it without needing to know the story.

grounding: A teenager publicly turned down at school writes poems and songs instead of lashing out, and one is chosen for the school magazine.

Dear Pallavi,
You asked if I'm okay after Vivek said he "didn't feel that way". Honestly? The first night I wanted to message him something horrible. I even typed it. Then I deleted it and wrote a song instead. It's called "Seen at 9:42", because that's when he read my message and didn't reply. It's only four lines and a chorus, but when I sang it to myself on the terrace, I cried, and it felt... cleaner? Like the feeling had somewhere to live that wasn't my stomach.
I've written six poems since. One is funny, about me practising in the mirror what I'd say to him. I'm sending you two. Please don't show anyone. Okay, maybe show your brother.
Love,
Your cousin-sister Himani

qa.q: What is Himani's song called?
qa.a: "Seen at 9:42".

qa.q: What did Himani feel on the first night, and how did the song change it?
qa.a: She was hurt enough to want to send something horrible; singing the song let her cry and made the feeling 'cleaner', as if it had somewhere to live.

qa.q: What choice on the first night made the difference?
qa.a: Deleting the horrible message and writing a song instead, which turned the hurt into something she could shape and share.

qa.q: What might Pallavi feel on receiving the two poems?
qa.a: Trusted and relieved that Himani is coping, and perhaps touched to be let into something so private.

grounding: A teenage girl writes to her cousin that after a rejection she deleted a cruel message and wrote a song and poems instead.

Jyoti, you asked why I've been scribbling in every free period. Okay. Remember Kabir? After farewell practice I finally told him I liked him. He said, "You're a really good friend, Ankita," and walked back to the others. Friend. That word sat on me for days.
I wanted to post something mean about him. I had it typed. Then I thought, no, I'll write how it actually feels. So I did. In Hindi, because it hurt in Hindi. Eleven lines about waiting at the bus stop for a message that doesn't come.
Yesterday Ma'am read it and asked if she could put it in the school magazine, without names. And you know what's strange? Now that it's on paper, it doesn't feel like it's only mine. Riya from 9C came up and said, "That's exactly it."

qa.q: What did Kabir say after farewell practice?
qa.a: "You're a really good friend, Ankita."

qa.q: Why did Ankita decide to write instead of posting the mean message?
qa.a: Ankita wanted to say how it actually felt rather than hurt Kabir, and writing let the pain come out honestly without lashing out.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the heartbreak felt?
qa.a: Deleting the typed post and writing the eleven lines in Hindi; once the poem was on paper and shared, the pain had a shape and others could recognise it.

qa.q: What does Riya's "That's exactly it" suggest about how the poem reached others?
qa.a: Riya seems to have felt something similar, so the poem turned a private hurt into something shared and less lonely 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager rejected by a classmate choosing to write a poem instead of a mean post, giving the hurt a shape that others can see and share.

I'm Nikita, Gautam's neighbour on the third floor. We've walked to tuition together since Class 6, so I noticed when Gautam went quiet after Sneha said no to him at the Holi party. He didn't rant, didn't block her, didn't say one bad thing about her to anyone.
Instead, every evening I heard his old keyboard through the wall: the same few notes, over and over, and his voice trying words, stopping, trying again. His notebook, which used to be all physics, filled up with short lines crossed out and rewritten.
Three weeks later he played the song at our building's Sunday music evening. It was about a coloured handprint fading from a sleeve. He didn't look at anyone while he sang. Afterwards two aunties hugged him, and a boy from the fifth floor asked for the words.
I don't know if it hurt less. But he looked lighter.

qa.q: What was Gautam's song about?
qa.a: A coloured handprint fading from a sleeve.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling as he tried the words over and over?
qa.a: He was likely hurt by Sneha's no, and shaping it into a song gave the pain somewhere to go instead of turning it on her.

qa.q: Which choice after the Holi party worked well for Gautam?
qa.a: Not ranting or blocking Sneha but writing and rewriting the song, then sharing it, which gave the hurt a form others could see.

qa.q: Why might the boy from the fifth floor ask for the words?
qa.a: The song may have matched something the boy felt too, showing how Gautam's private hurt became something others could hold on to.

grounding: Illustrates, through a neighbour's eyes, a rejected teenager who turns heartbreak into a song instead of lashing out, and shares it with others.

passage: Arnab, you asked what that poem at the open mic was really about. Okay. Vaibhav's big confession. In class eleven I finally told Sana I liked her, after a year of practising in the mirror. She said no, kindly. "I don't feel the same." And I wanted to do something stupid. I wanted to post something mean, or tell everyone she'd led me on, which wasn't true. Instead I went home and wrote. Ten pages of the worst poetry you've ever read. "Your laugh is a train I missed." That kind of thing. But I kept writing, every night for two months. Some of it got better. That poem I read tonight was the eleventh version. People clapped. A girl came up after and said, "That's exactly how it felt for me." That's when I realised the hurt had turned into something I could hand to someone else.

qa.q: How many versions of the poem did Vaibhav write?
qa.a: The poem read tonight was the eleventh version.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav write poetry instead of posting something mean?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt hurt and tempted to lash out, but writing gave the pain a shape and a safe place to go.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's story suggest a teenager could try after a rejection?
qa.a: Putting the hurt into writing or songs, even badly at first, rather than attacking the person who said no.

qa.q: How might the girl who came up after the reading have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt understood and less alone, seeing her own heartbreak in Vaibhav's poem.

grounding: Shows a teenager who has been rejected writing poems instead of lashing out, turning the hurt into something others can share.

passage:
June: Nirmala told her closest friend Ritu that she wanted them to be best friends again, like in primary school. Ritu said, gently, that she had a new group now. Nirmala went home and cried into her pillow. She thought about sending Ritu an angry message. Instead she opened a notebook and wrote a poem called "The Bench We Shared."
July: Nirmala wrote a poem every night. Some were about Ritu. Some were about the empty bench. She set one to a tune on her cousin's guitar.
August: The school magazine asked for submissions. Nirmala sent in the bench poem. It was printed on page six. At break, a girl from class nine found her. "I read your poem. My best friend moved away. It's exactly that." Nirmala smiled. It still hurt. But the hurt had a shape now.

qa.q: On which page was Nirmala's poem printed?
qa.a: On page six.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala write a poem instead of sending the angry message?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, and writing gave the pain a shape without hurting Ritu.

qa.q: What did Nirmala gain by sending the poem to the magazine?
qa.a: She let others see her pain and found someone who felt the same, which made her feel less alone.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel if she read "The Bench We Shared"?
qa.a: Ritu might feel moved and a little sad, seeing how much the friendship had meant to Nirmala.

grounding: Shows a teenager rejected by a friend turning the hurt into poems and songs instead of lashing out, and others recognising the pain in them.

passage: Afreen, you're crying over that boy, and I can see you typing an angry message. Put the phone down for a minute. Let your Preeti Khala tell you. When I was sixteen, in Bhopal, I liked a boy from the next lane, Rizwan. I gave him a card. He laughed with his friends about it. I was so hurt I wanted to tell the whole school something ugly about him. Instead, my grandmother gave me her old harmonium and said, "Sing it." So I did. I made up a song, all about a card thrown in the wind. I sang it badly, every night, for weeks. Then I wrote more. By eighteen, I was singing at weddings, and one of those songs was that card song. People cried. I never did send that ugly message.

qa.q: What did young Preeti give Rizwan?
qa.a: A card.

qa.q: Why did young Preeti want to tell the school something ugly about Rizwan?
qa.a: She felt deeply hurt and humiliated when he laughed about the card, and the pain pushed her towards lashing out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her grandmother gave her the harmonium and said "Sing it," which let the pain go into songs instead of revenge.

qa.q: How might the wedding guests have felt hearing the card song?
qa.a: They were moved, some crying, because the song gave shape to a hurt many of them knew.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager turning rejection into songs instead of lashing out, making the pain something others could see.

Nazia found out on the crowded school bus, from a message Farhaan sent while sitting two rows ahead: "Sorry, I just see you as a friend." The bus lurched, everyone was loud, and she had a chemistry test in forty minutes.

She wanted to send him something cruel. She typed three angry lines, then deleted them. Instead she pulled out the back of her bus pass and wrote in tiny letters: "I was a lamp you walked past / on your way to somewhere bright."

She kept writing in the margin of her rough sheet after the test, then at lunch in the noisy canteen. By evening she had a whole poem. Two weeks later, at the school's poetry evening, Avni squeezed her hand as Nazia read it aloud. The room went silent, then clapped.

qa.q: What did Farhaan's message say?
qa.a: The message said, "Sorry, I just see you as a friend."

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she typed three angry lines?
qa.a: Nazia felt hurt and rejected and wanted to lash out, but chose to put that pain into lines of poetry instead.

qa.q: What went well about Nazia's way of coping?
qa.a: Writing gave the hurt a shape instead of a cruel message, and reading it aloud let others see and share it.

qa.q: How might Avni feel squeezing Nazia's hand at the poetry evening?
qa.a: Avni probably feels proud and protective, knowing how much the poem cost Nazia.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl rejected on a noisy bus before a test who turns the hurt into a poem instead of a cruel reply.

passage:
Hrithik had said no in the school corridor, kindly but clearly: "I like someone else." Himani nodded, said "cool, no problem", and walked straight to the girls' washroom.

At home in the Dwarka flat she didn't throw anything or post the angry status she had half-written about him. She took her cousin's old guitar onto the balcony, where the neighbours' washing flapped, and picked out the three chords she knew. Words came slowly: "You said it soft, it still hit hard."

She sang it under her breath for an hour, crossing out lines in her notebook, changing "hard" to "loud" and back. By Sunday there were two verses and a chorus. She played it for her sister, who went quiet and said, "That's really good. It sounds exactly how it feels."

qa.q: What did Hrithik say in the corridor?
qa.a: Hrithik said, "I like someone else."

qa.q: Why did Himani say "cool, no problem" and walk to the washroom?
qa.a: Himani felt hurt and embarrassed and didn't want Hrithik to see, so she hid the pain until she could be alone.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Himani, and why?
qa.a: Making a song instead of posting the angry status gave the hurt a shape and didn't harm anyone.

qa.q: How does Himani's sister see the song?
qa.a: The sister is moved and says it sounds exactly how it feels, so the song lets her understand Himani's pain.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl turned down by a classmate who writes a song on the balcony instead of posting an angry status.

"Okay, don't laugh," Gurleen said, holding out a crumpled page in the music room.
Maria read it. "Is this about Harman?"
"Maybe."
"He said no on Friday. I thought you'd be, like, raging."
"I was. I wanted to tell the whole group what he said about the trip." Gurleen shrugged. "I wrote this instead. Read the second verse."
Maria read aloud: "I kept your name like a coin in my pocket, / spent it on nothing, still can't let it go." Maria looked up. "Gurleen. This is actually sad. In a good way."
"Can we put a tune to it? The keyboard's free."
"Only if I get to do the chords."
They played it three times. By the last time, Gurleen was almost smiling.

qa.q: When did Harman say no?
qa.a: Harman said no on Friday.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling before writing the verses?
qa.a: Gurleen felt hurt and raging, wanting to tell the whole group about Harman, but turned that pain into a poem.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do instead of lashing out, and why does it help?
qa.a: Gurleen wrote verses and set them to music with Maria, which gave the hurt a shape and let a friend share it.

qa.q: How does Maria see the poem?
qa.a: Maria is surprised and moved, finding it sad in a good way, and wants to help make it a song.

grounding: Shows a teenager rejected by a boy who writes verses instead of spreading gossip, then turns them into a song with a friend.

passage: When Akash told me in Class 11 that he "only saw me as a friend", I wanted to do something dramatic. Delete his number, post something mean, tell everyone his secrets. I didn't. Thursday.
She said no. Nicely, but no. I walked home wanting to throw my phone into the canal. I wanted to write something awful on her page. I didn't. I sat on the roof and wrote lyrics on the back of my maths notebook instead. Line one was terrible. Line eight was okay. By dinner I had a whole song called "Paper Boats". I sent the words to Jomon, who plays guitar. He called back and said, "Okay, this is actually good." It still hurts. But now the hurt has a tune. We're going to record it on Sunday.
Tanvir
